claim: UNC-33 (CRMP) is important for neuronal development and microtubule organization.
source: Interestingly, one of the top-scoring partners of UNC-119, UNC-33 (CRMP), was reported to be important for neuronal development and microtubule organization (Maniar et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Maniar et al., 2012).

claim: UNC-33 has three isoforms in C. elegans: small (UNC-33S), medium (UNC-33M) and large (UNC-33L).
source: UNC-33 is a putative microtubule binding protein, which has three isoforms in C. elegans: small (UNC-33S), medium (UNC-33M) and large (UNC-33L)

claim: Only the large isoform of UNC-33 (UNC-33L) is able to rescue the neuronal polarity defects of the unc-33 mutant.

claim: UNC-33L, but not UNC33S, efficiently binds to UNC-119 in pull-down experiments in cultured Hek293T cells.
source: To validate and map the interaction between UNC-33 and UNC-119, we performed pull-down experiments in cultured Hek293T cells and found that the UNC-33L, but not UNC33S, efficiently binds to UNC-119 (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by pull-down experimental data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: UNC-119 binds to the UNC-33L specific N-terminus.
source: Moreover, UNC-119 was able to pull down the UNC-33L specific N-terminus (Figure 2B), further proving that the UNC-119 interacts with the UNC-33L isoform.
evidence: The claim is supported by pull-down experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: UNC-44 (Ankyrin) acts downstream of unc-33 (CRMP).
source: Previous work has shown that UNC-33 (CRMP) acts downstream of unc-44 (Ankyrin) and that the unc-44 mutant has very similar phenotypes as the unc-33 mutant (Harterink et al., 2018; Maniar et al., 2012; Meng et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Harterink et al., 2018; Maniar et al., 2012; Meng et al., 2016).

claim: The unc-44 mutant has very similar phenotypes as the unc-33 mutant.
source: Previous work has shown that UNC-33 (CRMP) acts downstream of unc-44 (Ankyrin) and that the unc-44 mutant has very similar phenotypes as the unc-33 mutant (Harterink et al., 2018; Maniar et al., 2012; Meng et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Harterink et al., 2018; Maniar et al., 2012; Meng et al., 2016).

claim: No direct interaction was detected between UNC-44 and UNC-33 by immunoprecipitation from Hek293T cells.
source: However, we failed to detect a direct interaction between UNC-44 and UNC-33 by immunoprecipitation from Hek293T cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: UNC-119 was identified as a possible binding partner for UNC-44 in a yeast two-hybrid screen.
source: In a yeast two-hybrid screen for C. elegans interacting proteins, UNC-119 was identified as a possible binding partner for UNC-44 (Li et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Li et al., 2004).

claim: UNC-119 bridges UNC-44 to UNC-33.
source: This, together with our finding that UNC-119 interacts with UNC-33, suggests that UNC-119 bridges UNC-44 to UNC-33.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the interaction data showing UNC-119 binds both UNC-44 and UNC-33.

claim: The UNC-44 C-terminus specifically binds to UNC-119 in Hek293T cells.
source: Using these fragments in Hek293T cells we found that the UNC-44 C-terminus specifically was able to bind to UNC-119 (Figure 2C), which is in agreement with the interaction domain identified by the yeast two-hybrid screen (Li et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by pull-down experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The UNC-44 C-terminus interaction with UNC-119 is in agreement with the interaction domain identified by the yeast two-hybrid screen.
source: Using these fragments in Hek293T cells we found that the UNC-44 C-terminus specifically was able to bind to UNC-119 (Figure 2C), which is in agreement with the interaction domain identified by the yeast two-hybrid screen (Li et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparing current data with previous yeast two-hybrid results (Li et al., 2004).

claim: UNC-33L only binds to UNC-44 in the presence of UNC-119.
source: We again found that UNC-119 efficiently binds to the UNC-44 C-terminus, however UNC-33L only binds to UNC-44 in the presence of UNC-119 (Figure 2D), showing that UNC-33L, UNC-44, and UNC-119 together can form a ternary complex (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by pull-down experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: UNC-33L, UNC-44, and UNC-119 together can form a ternary complex.
source: We again found that UNC-119 efficiently binds to the UNC-44 C-terminus, however UNC-33L only binds to UNC-44 in the presence of UNC-119 (Figure 2D), showing that UNC-33L, UNC-44, and UNC-119 together can form a ternary complex (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by pull-down experimental data shown in Figure 2D and the model in Figure 2E.

claim: Mutants for unc-33, unc-44, and unc-119 have very similar phenotypes.
source: Since mutants for each of these three unc-genes have very similar phenotypes and that the corresponding proteins can form a complex strongly suggests that UNC-33L, UNC-44, and UNC-119 have a common function in neuronal development.
evidence: The claim is based on observations of phenotypes in the mutants.

claim: UNC-33L, UNC-44, and UNC-119 have a common function in neuronal development.
source: Since mutants for each of these three unc-genes have very similar phenotypes and that the corresponding proteins can form a complex strongly suggests that UNC-33L, UNC-44, and UNC-119 have a common function in neuronal development.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the similar phenotypes and the ability to form a complex.

claim: The giant AO13 Ankyrin splice isoform is essential for neuronal development.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Boontrakulpoontawee and Otsuka, 2002; Otsuka et al., 2002).

claim: UNC-44::GFP mainly localizes to axons and dendrites.
source: UNC-44::GFP mainly localizes to axons and dendrites and its expression pattern is nearly indistinguishable from the UNC-119::GFP knock-in (Figure 3B).

claim: The expression pattern of UNC-44::GFP is nearly indistinguishable from the UNC-119::GFP knock-in.
source: UNC-44::GFP mainly localizes to axons and dendrites and its expression pattern is nearly indistinguishable from the UNC-119::GFP knock-in (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data comparing UNC-44::GFP and UNC-119::GFP expression patterns.

claim: UNC-44::GFP clearly localizes to the cortex.
source: We observed that UNC-44::GFP clearly localizes to the cortex (Figure 3C)

claim: UNC-44 is expected to be immobile as a protein that is part of cortical cytoskeleton.
source: and that it is highly immobile by FRAP in axons and dendrites (Figure 3D–F), as expected from a protein that is part of cortical cytoskeleton (Bennett and Lorenzo, 2016)
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about cortical cytoskeleton proteins, supported by citation (Bennett and Lorenzo, 2016).

claim: UNC-119 immobility is not affected in the unc-33 mutant.

claim: UNC-33S and UNC-33M are enriched in the cell body compared to UNC-33L.

source: Ankyrin proteins are well-characterized component of the cortical actin-spectrin cytoskeleton (Bennett and Baines, 2001)
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge, supported by citation (Bennett and Baines, 2001).

claim: The cortical actin-spectrin cytoskeleton forms a characteristic periodic cytoskeleton in invertebrate and vertebrate neurons.
source: which forms a characteristic periodic cytoskeleton in invertebrate (Krieg et al., 2017) and vertebrate neurons (Xu et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge, supported by citations (Krieg et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2013).

claim: UNC-44::GFP (Ankyrin) forms a periodic assembly similar to the 180–200 nm pattern observed with YFP::UNC-70 (β-spectrin).

evidence: The claim is supported by TIRF-SIM imaging data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: UNC-119::GFP shows a ~200 nm periodic pattern that corresponds well with the observed UNC-44 distribution.

claim: UNC-33L shows periodicity in striking similarity to UNC-119 and UNC-44.

claim: UNC-33M does not show a periodic pattern.

evidence: The claim is supported by TIRF-SIM imaging data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The ternary UNC-44/UNC-119/UNC-33L complex shares a stereotypic periodic pattern similar to the cortical spectrin cytoskeleton.
source: Taken together, the ternary UNC-44/UNC-119/UNC-33L complex shares a stereotypic periodic pattern similar to the cortical spectrin cytoskeleton.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the TIRF-SIM imaging data showing periodic patterns for all three proteins.

claim: CRMPs are described as cytosolic phosphoproteins that can bind microtubules via their C-terminus.
source: CRMPs are described as cytosolic phosphoproteins that can bind microtubules via their C-terminus (Lin et al., 2011; Niwa et al., 2017; Zheng et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge, supported by citations (Lin et al., 2011; Niwa et al., 2017; Zheng et al., 2018).

claim: Both UNC-33S::GFP and UNC-33L::GFP efficiently bind to microtubules when ectopically expressed in hypodermal seam cells.
source: To increase subcellular resolution, we ectopically expressed UNC-33S::GFP and UNC-33L::GFP in the hypodermal seam cells and found that both efficiently bind to microtubules and that the C-terminus is indeed essential for this interaction (Figure 5A and B; Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: The C-terminus of UNC-33 is essential for microtubule binding.
source: To increase subcellular resolution, we ectopically expressed UNC-33S::GFP and UNC-33L::GFP in the hypodermal seam cells and found that both efficiently bind to microtubules and that the C-terminus is indeed essential for this interaction (Figure 5A and B; Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data showing loss of microtubule binding when C-terminus is deleted, as shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Upon loss of microtubule binding, UNC-33L partially relocalizes to the cortex, whereas the shorter UNC-33S does not.
source: Interestingly, we observed that upon loss of microtubule binding, UNC-33L partially relocalizes to the cortex, whereas the shorter UNC-33S does not.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data showing differential localization of UNC-33L and UNC-33S upon loss of C-terminus.

claim: The cortical relocalization of UNC-33L upon loss of microtubule binding depends on UNC-44 and UNC-119.
source: Indeed, we found that the cortical relocalization of UNC-33L upon loss of microtubule binding depends on UNC-44 and UNC-119 (Figure 5B; Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data in mutant backgrounds shown in Figure 5B.

claim: UNC-33SΔC and UNC-33MΔC rapidly recover in FRAP analysis.
source: With FRAP analysis, we found that UNC-33SΔC and UNC-33MΔC rapidly recover (Figure 5C–G), which indicates that the immobile pool of UNC-33S and UNC-33M (Figure 3N-P) is the result of microtubule binding.
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP experimental data shown in Figure 5C–G.

claim: The immobile pool of UNC-33S and UNC-33M is the result of microtubule binding.
source: With FRAP analysis, we found that UNC-33SΔC and UNC-33MΔC rapidly recover (Figure 5C–G), which indicates that the immobile pool of UNC-33S and UNC-33M (Figure 3N-P) is the result of microtubule binding.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the FRAP data showing that deletion of the microtubule-binding C-terminus eliminates the immobile pool.

claim: UNC-33LΔC is still highly immobile despite lacking the microtubule-binding C-terminus.
source: UNC-33LΔC however, is still highly immobile (Figure 5B, H and I).
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP experimental data shown in Figure 5B, H and I.

claim: Binding to microtubules via the C-terminus is essential for UNC-33L functioning.

evidence: The claim is supported by rescue data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Binding to microtubules via the C-terminus is not required for UNC-33L immobilization.
source: This suggests that although binding to microtubules via the C-terminus is essential for UNC-33L functioning (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), it is not required for its immobilization.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the FRAP data showing UNC-33LΔC remains immobile.

claim: UNC-33LΔC signal rapidly recovers in the unc-119 mutant.
source: The UNC-33LΔC signal rapidly recovers in the unc-119 mutant (Figure 5J and K), which shows that UNC-119 binds to the N-terminus to immobilize UNC-33L to UNC-44.
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP experimental data in the unc-119 mutant shown in Figure 5J and K.

claim: UNC-119 binds to the N-terminus to immobilize UNC-33L to UNC-44.
source: The UNC-33LΔC signal rapidly recovers in the unc-119 mutant (Figure 5J and K), which shows that UNC-119 binds to the N-terminus to immobilize UNC-33L to UNC-44.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the FRAP data showing UNC-33LΔC becomes mobile in the unc-119 mutant.

claim: In neurons, UNC-33L stably associates with microtubules via its C-terminus and to the cortex through its N-terminal interaction with UNC-119.
source: Together, these results indicate that in neurons UNC-33L stably associates with microtubules via its C-terminus and to the cortex through its N-terminal interaction with UNC-119.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combination of microtubule binding data and FRAP dynamics data.

claim: The stability of the UNC-44/119/33 complex and the attachment of the microtubule binding UNC-33L (CRMP) to the cortex suggests that the complex anchors microtubules in neurons.
source: The stability of the UNC-44/119/33 complex and the attachment of the microtubule binding UNC-33L (CRMP) to the cortex, suggests that the complex anchors microtubules in neurons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the stability data and cortical localization of the complex.

claim: Microtubules are evenly distributed over the primary dendrites and the axon in wild type PVD neurons.
source: To visualize the microtubule cytoskeleton we expressed the microtubule binding protein MAPH-1 in the PVD neuron (Harterink et al., 2018) and found that microtubules are evenly distributed over the primary dendrites and the axon in wild type animals (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6A.
